title: Merge User Identities
summary: Merge customer records from several systems into unique people via shared emails.

stages.title: Merge identities
stages.requirement:
Each record from our CRM, billing and support systems is `[name, email1, email2, ...]`.
Two records belong to the same person if they share **any** email, and that sharing is
transitive. Write `merge_identities(records)` returning one list per person:
`[name, *emails]` with the person's distinct emails **sorted**.

- Use the name from the **earliest record** (lowest index) in the group.
- Order people by the index of their earliest record.
- Emails compare case-insensitively and are output **lowercased**.
- A record may have no emails. It is then its own person, `[name]`.

```python
merge_identities([
    ["Ada", "ada@x.com", "a@y.com"],
    ["Bob", "bob@x.com"],
    ["Ada L.", "A@Y.com", "ada@z.com"],
])
# -> [["Ada", "a@y.com", "ada@x.com", "ada@z.com"], ["Bob", "bob@x.com"]]
```

Up to 20,000 records with up to 10 emails each.

visibleTests.name: test_example
visibleTests.code:
def test_example():
    records = [
        ["Ada", "ada@x.com", "a@y.com"],
        ["Bob", "bob@x.com"],
        ["Ada L.", "A@Y.com", "ada@z.com"],
    ]
    assert merge_identities(records) == [["Ada", "a@y.com", "ada@x.com", "ada@z.com"], ["Bob", "bob@x.com"]]

hiddenTests.name: test_large_chain
hiddenTests.description: Recursive DFS over 20k records hits the recursion limit, so use iteration or union-find.
hiddenTests.code:
def test_large_chain():
    records = [[f"P{i}", f"e{i}@x", f"e{i + 1}@x"] for i in range(20_000)]
    out = merge_identities(records)
    assert len(out) == 1
    assert out[0][0] == "P0"
    assert len(out[0]) == 20_002

hints: Think of records as nodes connected when they share an email. You want the connected components.
Union-find works well: map each lowercased email to the first record that used it, and union later records with that one.
Union by the smaller index (or track each component's minimum record index) to get the earliest name and the output order. Avoid recursion depth issues with iterative `find`.

solution.explanation:
Records sharing an email are unioned. An `email -> first record` map keeps that linear
rather than pairwise. Making the smaller index the root means every component's root is
its earliest record, which gives both the name to use and the output order. `find` is
iterative with path compression, so 20k-long chains don't overflow the stack.
solution.timeComplexity: O(E α(n)) for E total emails
